title: Bengal's new industry policy thinks outside the box: Pooling land to taking back unused land
syllabus: GS3 › Land reforms; Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Investment models · GS2 › Government policies and interventions (state); e-governance and transparency · GS4 › Fairness and transparency in land allotment
summary: West Bengal's Investment Promotion Policy, 2026 proposes direct purchase of land, land pooling and taking back unused industrial land, with production required within three years of allotment.
ideas: Land is the binding constraint: large contiguous plots are not available as land is fragmented into small holdings, so pooling is proposed to create large areas for major industries.
GS3 · Land reforms / industrial policy
Fragmented holdings make land the main bottleneck to industry, which land pooling seeks to solve.
Consent over coercion: the state wants to buy land directly rather than acquire it ('We do not want another Singur or Nandigram'), learning from the movements that ended the Left Front's rule.
GS3 · Land acquisition / GS2 · Governance
Bengal's shift from acquisition to purchase and pooling reflects the political lesson of Singur and Nandigram: consent sustains industry.
Use it or lose it: production must begin within three years of allotment, land cannot be used for other purposes, unused industrial land will be recovered, and brownfield redevelopment gets priority.
GS3 · Efficient use of land
A three-year 'use it or lose it' clause stops land hoarding by investors.

Transparency by design: a GIS-enabled inventory of industrial land (ownership, plot size, use, connectivity, utilities, encumbrances), published criteria, online applications, time-stamped scrutiny and disclosure of decisions.
GS2 · E-governance and transparency
A GIS land inventory with online, time-stamped allotment cuts discretion and the scope for corruption.

Safeguards and inclusion: land support does not exempt units from land-use, environment, rehabilitation, tenancy, forest or coastal laws; the policy favours labour-intensive industries and MSMEs employing more women and transgender people. Pooling terms are yet to be detailed.
GS3 · Inclusive industrialisation
Land support must not bypass rehabilitation and environmental law, or today's investment becomes tomorrow's Singur.
keywords: Landowners pool plots for development and get back a share of developed land or benefits
Land pooling makes landowners partners in development rather than displaced sellers.
Reusing previously developed or idle industrial land
Brownfield redevelopment brings industry without taking new farmland.
A government-maintained inventory of land ready for allotment
A GIS land bank cuts the time investors spend searching for land.
A condition that allotted land must be used within a set time or be taken back
Use-it-or-lose-it clauses turn allotted land into factories, not speculation.
examples: 'No more Singur or Nandigram'
Bengal shifts from acquisition to direct purchase and pooling
GS4
GS3 · Land acquisition · GS4 · Consent and fairness
Singur and Nandigram remain India's lesson that industry built without consent cannot last.
GIS-enabled industrial land inventory
Online, time-stamped allotment with disclosed decisions
GS4
GS2 · E-governance · GS4 · Transparency
A public, GIS-based land inventory is an example of technology reducing discretion in allotment.
pyqs: Key issues addressed by the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
Why industrial growth lagged GDP after reforms; can recent industrial policy changes help?
Manufacturing's share in GDP, especially MSMEs; present policies.
Drafting a fair compensation-cum-rehabilitation policy for persons displaced by projects.

trend.t: Land questions have tested the 2013 land acquisition law (2014) and, repeatedly, land reforms in agriculture (2013, 2016, 2021, 2023, 2024). Industrial policy questions asked why manufacturing lags (2017, 2023). GS4 asked for a fair rehabilitation policy (2016).
trend.watch: Land reforms recur most years in GS3, so land is a must-study area; questions on land for industry, consent and rehabilitation can draw on new state policies such as pooling.
focus: Land acquisition vs land pooling vs direct purchase
Land as a constraint on manufacturing

potential: "Land pooling is a more democratic alternative to land acquisition." Critically examine. (10 marks)

title: PM hails nod for VISTAR scheme to modernise statistical system
syllabus: GS2 › Government policies and interventions; e-governance and transparency · GS3 › Indian economy: planning and growth (data for policy)
summary: The Cabinet approved the Rs 4,371.1-crore VISTAR scheme, a central sector scheme to 2030-31, to modernise India's official statistics using technology and AI.
ideas: Better data, better decisions: the PM said better data would lead to better decisions, improved policy-making and more effective delivery of services.
GS2 · Evidence-based governance
VISTAR reflects a simple truth of governance: policies are only as good as the data behind them.
Modern, integrated statistics: the scheme will use technology and AI, strengthen micro-level data collection and build integrated statistical systems.
GS2 · E-governance
Micro-level, AI-enabled statistics can help target welfare to the household and village level.
Closing data gaps: the same day's ASI data show no gender break-up of contract workers, the kind of gap modern statistics must fill.
GS2 · Statistics / GS1 · Gender data
From contract workers to women's work, India's data gaps show why statistical reform matters.
keywords: Designing policy on reliable data and evaluation
VISTAR can strengthen evidence-based policy by giving faster, finer data.
A scheme fully funded and implemented by the Union government
As a central sector scheme, VISTAR is fully funded by the Centre.
examples: VISTAR (Rs 4,371.1 crore, to 2030-31)
AI, micro-level data and integrated statistical systems
GS2 · E-governance · GS4 · Rational decision-making
VISTAR is a ready example of using technology to improve the quality of public decisions.
pyqs: Digital technology as a reliable source of input for rational decision-making.

trend.t: Data and technology for decision-making have been asked mainly in GS4 (digital technology in 2021, AI in 2024), and data protection in GS3 (2018, 2024).
trend.watch: The use of technology for rational decisions was asked in GS4 in 2021 and 2024; statistical reform is a useful example for both.

potential: "Good governance begins with good data." Discuss with reference to recent steps to modernise India's statistical system. (10 marks)

title: Challenge is wages, not jobs. Expanding Jan Vishwas interventions can help
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Manish Sabharwal, Teamlease Services)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Growth and development · GS2 › Government policies; Transparency and accountability; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: After decriminalising thousands of offences, the writer argues the next Jan Vishwas phase should make every rule published, knowable and trust-based, because India's problem is low wages, not a lack of jobs.
ideas: Wages, not jobs: India's problem is job quality, not quantity; a third of the workforce is in employed poverty, trapped in informal wage work and self-employment.
GS3 · Employment
India's employment challenge is low-wage informality, not joblessness; the fix lies in formal, high-wage job creation.
Regulatory cholesterol: China's per-capita GDP is five times India's (on par in 1991), not because of effort but because of India's lack of transparency, consistency and trust in law enforcement.
GS3 · Growth / GS2 · Governance
Regulatory cholesterol, not lack of talent or effort, explains much of India's per-capita income gap with China.

Six toxic thought worlds: prior approval (prohibited till permitted), enforcing the unenforceable, process as punishment, blindness to 25+ instruments below Acts, laws for edge cases, and excessive criminalisation.
GS2 · Administrative reform
India's regulatory mindset (prior approval, process as punishment, over-criminalisation) treats the citizen as a suspect.

Three next steps: Siddhant (trust-based regulation on freedom, necessity, proportionality, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants), Sangreh (a single legal record as DPI) and Ashwasan (only published obligations are enforceable).
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to trust, knowability and certainty through Siddhant, Sangreh and Ashwasan.

Law must be knowable: ignorance of law is no excuse only if the State makes law accessible; earlier attempts failed on design, capacity, fragmented power, attention and technology, and lacked a binding duty to publish.
GS2 · Rule of law / Transparency
A citizen's duty to obey the law presupposes the State's duty to publish it; unpublished rules breed uncertainty and corruption.
keywords: Accumulated rules, filings and permissions that clog enterprise
Regulatory cholesterol raises the cost of formality and pushes firms into informality.
Employed poverty shows India's real problem is wage quality, not job quantity.
A prohibited-till-permitted regime presumes guilt and slows enterprise.
The procedure itself harasses the innocent
When process is punishment, even compliant citizens bear the cost of regulation.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse
Ignorantia juris holds only when the State makes the law knowable.
One machine-readable source for every legal obligation (Sangreh)
A legal DPI like Sangreh can do for compliance what UPI did for payments.
examples: Supreme Court on knowable law
Harla v State of Rajasthan (1952) rejected secret laws; B K Srinivasan (1987) moved to knowability; Viraj Impex (2019) held law operative only when published
GS2 · Judiciary / Rule of law
From Harla (1952) to Viraj Impex (2019), courts have held unpublished law cannot bind citizens.
Global single-source registers
US Federal Register, UK legislation.gov.uk, EU EUR-Lex, Singapore Statutes Online
GS2 · Comparative governance
Democracies like the US, UK and Singapore publish all binding rules in one register; India's Sangreh can follow.
Transparency of Rules Act (TORA)
Sanjeev Sanyal's draft: every enforceable obligation must be published on Sangreh
GS4
GS2 · Transparency / GS4 · Probity
TORA would make publication a precondition for enforcement, curbing discretion and corruption.
Adam Smith and the Constitution
250 years of The Wealth of Nations, 76 of the Constitution: both see government as expanding freedom
GS2 · Constitutional values / Essay
Both Adam Smith and the Constitution see the State as an enabler of freedom, not its gatekeeper.
pyqs: Trust through rule of law: Sangreh and Ashwasan are trust tools.
Job-rich, productive growth: formal high-wage jobs through deregulation.
Informalisation: regulatory cholesterol as a cause.
Civil servant as enabler: Siddhant's adoption by civil servants.

trend.t: Governance questions moved from regulatory autonomy (2015) to the e-governance interactive model (2024) and trust built through rule of law and participation (2026). Employment moved from informalisation (2016) to job-rich, productive growth (2022). GS4 (2025) asks the civil servant to be an enabler, not a regulator.
trend.watch: 'Trust' is the new keyword in GS2 and GS4. Prepare trust-based, citizen-centric governance with examples such as Jan Vishwas, GST arrest powers and self-certification.
focus: Rule of law: knowability of law

potential: "India's challenge is not jobs but wages." Examine, and suggest reforms to promote formal, high-wage employment. (15 marks)
Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed? (10 marks)
"The citizen's duty to know the law presupposes the State's duty to make it knowable." Comment. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed?

answer.t: Jan Vishwas has decriminalised thousands of offences, yet a third of India's workforce remains in employed poverty, held back by regulatory cholesterol.

pts.t: The State treats citizens and firms as honest stakeholders, not suspects.
Fewer jail terms for minor lapses reduce the fear of becoming formal.
Less 'process is punishment' lets firms combine land, labour and capital.
Less discretion means fewer chances for rent-seeking.
It attacks the root of informality.
Freedom, necessity and proportionality to guide regulation, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants.
One machine-readable legal DPI, unifying gazettes and India Code.
Only published obligations should be enforceable.
Periodic pruning of circulars and rules.

answer.t: Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to certainty, so that what is wrong with India's regulation is fixed by what is right with its democracy.

title: Retirement fund body unveils services to ease provident fund access; Digi Yatra trials for overseas flyers
where: Economy, page 10 (ENS Economic Bureau; Briefly, PTI)
syllabus: GS2 › E-governance: applications, models, successes; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Empathy and compassion in public service
summary: Minor topic: EPFO launched verified WhatsApp services and automatic settlement of small inoperative accounts; Digi Yatra trials for international passengers began at seven airports.
ideas: Services where people already are: EPFO's verified WhatsApp service gives PF balance, transactions and passbook, and guidance on the Employment Linked Incentive scheme, reducing office visits.
GS2 · E-governance
Delivering services on familiar platforms like WhatsApp makes e-governance truly citizen-centric.
From claims to automatic delivery: Aadhaar-verified inoperative EPF accounts with balances up to ₹1,000 will be settled without individual claims.
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Automatic settlement shifts the burden from the citizen to the State, the essence of proactive governance.
Human sensitivity in social security: the Labour Minister said every worker's grievance must be met with compassion and empathy, treating workers as nation-builders.
GS4 · Empathy in public service
Social security administration must combine efficiency with empathy for the worker.
Paperless travel goes international: Digi Yatra trials for Indian e-passport holders on select international flights have begun at seven airports, with wider rollout expected in 2027.
GS2 · E-governance / GS3 · Infrastructure
Digi Yatra shows digital public infrastructure extending from domestic to international travel.
keywords: No-claim settlement is proactive delivery: the State reaches the citizen first.
Services on platforms citizens already use
WhatsApp-based services improve last-mile digital access.
examples: EPFO WhatsApp and auto-settlement
Verified WhatsApp services; small inoperative accounts settled without claims
GS4
GS2 · E-governance, citizen-centric governance · GS4 · Innovation and empathy in public service
EPFO's WhatsApp service and no-claim settlement show innovation in public service that saves citizens time and trips.
Digi Yatra for international flyers
Trials at Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Cochin, Mumbai, Chennai and Amritsar
GS2 · E-governance · GS3 · Infrastructure
Digi Yatra's international trials show digital identity easing travel, while raising data-protection questions.
pyqs: E-governance beyond technology: the interactive service model.
